newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African maize prices seen easing this year.
newsitem.headline: S.African maize prices seen easing this year.

text.p: South African maize prices are expected to ease this year despite an expected smaller crop, weighed down by lower U.S. prices, increased global exports and a deregulated local market, industry sources said on Wednesday.

They said producer prices for maize could fall as low as 500 rand a tonne as domestic supply remained plentiful with around one million tonnes left over from last season's bumper harvest topped up by imports in the Western Cape province.
"The main reason for the downward trend in the world price is the bumper U.S. crop," said Andre Ferreira, senior economist at the National Maize Producers Organisation.
Ferreira said that the long term average world maize price was $110 a tonne, down from $135 in March and well below last year when global shortages spurred highs of around $200.
Rand prices for maize, South Africa's key agricultural commodity, were seen further depressed by a stronger rand/dollar exchange rate.
Although Ferreira did not expect payments to South African producers to fall below 550 rand, other industry players saw them as low as 500 rand if farmers began harvesting simultaneously.

"Because there is lots of maize being carried over, people will not have to buy in early. It will not be impossible for prices to go down to 500 rand a tonne, especially if farmers all start harvesting in May and June," said a maize trader.

"There is also less demand as it is cheaper for the Western Cape -- which is far from the maize belt -- to import. They are expected to import between 1.5 and two million tonnes this season," he said.

Bids for white and yellow maize futures on the South African Futures Exchange are down around 80 rand a tonne from highs in February when fears of a drought-hit crop abounded. At 1330 GMT July yellow contracts were bid at 605 rand and white at 595 rand.

Other factors leaning on prices included heavy exports by Argentinia and the complete deregulation of the South African market from May 1. Until now the state-owned Maize Board has fixed floor prices in the export market.
"The (board's) stabilisation fund tended to influence the market and pushed prices higher than they should have," said Hamish McBain, executive director at food and milling group Tiger Oats Ltd.
Although official estimates put the 1997 crop at two million tonnes below last year's 9.5 million, it is still well in surplus and not seen exerting upward pressure on prices.
Some players said the government forecast may have underestimated the size of the harvest as it did not include maize grown in former homelands.
"You're looking at a crop estimate given at 7.5 million tonnes, when in fact the real crop is in excess of 8.5, maybe as much as nine million tonnes," McBain said.
The U.S. Agriculture Department earlier this month forecast the crop at 8.5 million tonnes.
